items.title: Welcome to the machine: emulating a CPU
items.author: John Arundel
items.content:
Welcome to the Situation Room, . Thank you for coming in at such short notice. Eleven hours and sixteen minutes ago, our scientists lost contact with the Trailblazer 1 probe, en route to Proxima Centauri. Since then we’ve been trying without success to re-establish contact with the spacecraft’s onboard computer. Unless the fault can be rectified, and soon, we are facing a total loss of the vehicle and mission.

The binary data modulated onto the optical carrier signal suddenly changed from valid telemetry to a meaningless string of 1s. Since we’re still receiving the signal, we know the spacecraft is intact, powered, and with its communication laser aimed correctly towards Earth. Doppler radar data indicates that its trajectory is unchanged, making it unlikely that the craft was hit by a meteorite or space debris. It’s just no longer able to talk to us.

The problem appears to be localised to a subsystem known as the (Remote Telemetry and Flight Management) computer, responsible for the communications link between the spacecraft and Earth. Engineers are speculating that its memory may have been corrupted by a cosmic ray impact, causing the software to malfunction.

Unfortunately, it seems that while the probe’s computers and flight software were thoroughly documented before launch, that documentation is no longer available, due to… well, let’s just say . We also no longer have the source code or any way to reproduce it. It seems that these files were deleted when one of our cloud drives ran low on space, and everybody thought some department had a copy.

That’s where you come in. We urgently need your help to investigate the RTFM software issue. Specifically, the first thing we need is a program that can execute code written for the spacecraft’s onboard computer. A program like this is called an : it acts like a model of the computer’s central processing unit (), and will enable us to write and test code before uploading it to the RTFM for real. Time is running out, and there’s no room for mistakes: a botched software update could put the probe out of action for good.

You might also have heard the term , meaning not “nearly a machine”, but something more like “not actually a machine, but behaving like one”. Emulator, virtual machine, same thing.

It may sound complicated, but emulators are actually fairly easy to write, once you understand how the emulated machine (the ) works. The RTFM computer uses a relatively small and simple CPU, compared to the one in your computer (the machine).

This CPU is called the , and to emulate it, you’ll be writing the necessary code to implement the R8’s : the commands it understands. You can use any programming language you like to do this, but I have starter repos set up for Go and Rust if you’re using one of those:

Sebastián Alvarez has kindly provided a starter repo in TypeScript, too:

These repos will give you the basic structure of the project, plus some tests and stub functions to get you up and running, but after that it’s entirely up to you what to do. So if you want to use a language other than those provided, you could look at one of these repos to get the general idea, and start by implementing it in your language of choice.

The first thing the emulator needs is a properly-initialised CPU, ready to work. So, in the Go repo, for example, there’s an function that returns a CPU in its default initial state, which is specified by a test. In the Rust repo you’ll find an implementation of for the CPU that does the same thing.

The test and the constructor function are already provided in the starter repo, so your first challenge is a straightforward one:

Run the test and make sure it passes.

In Go, for example, run , or in Rust run .

The CPU is the heart of any computer: it does the data processing, executes the software, and controls every other part of the system. Usually made up of many and other electronic components on a , each different model of CPU understands a different . This consists of commands like “add this number to this other number”, “read the value at this memory address”, “jump to the program starting at this other address”, and so on.

Machine language is much than a programming language such as Go or Rust: it deals directly with the hardware on the chip. All the same, there are many similarities, and programs in Go and other high-level languages are usually —translated—into the equivalent —program in machine language.

Putting two and two together

For example, here’s a short program that a CPU such as the R8 might execute:

Can you guess what it does? That’s right, it adds 2 and 2. The (load) instruction puts a number into the CPU’s working area, or scratchpad (known as a ). In this case, it loads the number 2.

Then the instruction adds number to what’s already in the register. In this case, it adds the number 2. The result, if everything’s working correctly, is that the register should contain the value 4.

The R8 doesn’t understand words like or , though: those are (from the Greek for “remember”) designed to be easy for humans to read and write. Actual machine language just consists of numbers.

Every R8 instruction has its own unique identifying number: instruction number 1, instruction number 2, and so on. These are called (for “operation codes”). For example, the opcode for is 16, and the opcode for is 80. (Don’t worry about these particular numbers; they’re essentially arbitrary, like phone numbers.)

So the “add 2 and 2” program we just saw actually looks like this in machine language:

You can see why mnemonics were invented! It would be awfully difficult to write programs using only numbers, even though that’s the language that the R8 (like all CPUs) actually speaks. Instead, we use the symbolic names like and , giving us what’s called (I’m not sure why: maybe because writing programs is a bit like putting together IKEA furniture?)

We know that R8 programs are a sequence of numbers, but where do these numbers actually live in the computer, and how does the CPU know where to find them?

Another important component of every computer is : also a silicon chip, but a different kind of chip from a CPU. Its job is not to do anything, but just to store numbers: opcodes, operands, science data, images, or anything else we want the computer to handle.

Memory is arranged very simply: it’s just a sequence of —places you can store a number—each with its own , which is also a number. Think of memory addresses as being just like postal addresses. Address 66, for example, is like “Number 66, Memory Street, Computerville”. It contains a number, which may or may not be an opcode for a machine instruction, or an operand, or just zero because it’s currently unoccupied.

Even though a CPU might seem complicated, and in detail it is, it’s very simple in principle. It just does one thing, over and over, forever:

  1. Fetch the next instruction from memory

It’s called the . And that’s all your emulator needs to do: fetch the next instruction, and execute it. Let’s take the first part first.

Saying ‘the instruction’ implies that we have some way of remembering where we currently ‘are’ in memory. That is to say, we need a CPU register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to execute.

This is what the register is for (PC stands for ‘Program Counter’, which is the traditional name for this register). It keeps track of where the CPU is in the program.

Suppose holds 0, for example. If the CPU were to start running now, the first thing it would do would be to read the contents of memory address 0 (we say that to this address). It will interpret this as an opcode, and do whatever that opcode tells it to do. Afterwards, it will (add 1 to it), and the cycle begins again: the CPU will read the contents of memory address 1, interpret it as an opcode, and… well, you know the rest.

And that’s what your emulator will do, too: perform this fetch-execute cycle continuously. For testing and debugging purposes, though, we’ll start by just fetching and executing instruction at a time. And let’s choose a very easy instruction to implement: the instruction (short for “no operation”). It does nothing!

(Why have such an instruction in the first place, you might ask? Good question, and not every CPU has , but the R8 does. One use for it is just to pass the time, for example if you wanted the machine to wait for a specified delay period without doing anything. Anyway, it’s a good choice for our first emulated instruction.)

We’ll need a way for users to tell the machine to do one iteration of its fetch-execute cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory at the address held by , execute it, and return. So there’s a method on the CPU named that will do this.

Let’s see how we might use it to execute the instruction. First, we’ll call to create a freshly-initialised CPU.

Next, we need to load the program into memory. It’s only one instruction long, so we just need to put the opcode for the instruction (which is 1) into some memory location. Since starts at 0, let’s use memory address 0.

Now we call , which will do the following:

  1. Read the contents of memory at the address held by (which is currently 0).
  2. Interpret that value as an opcode, and do what it instructs (the value will be 1, which is the opcode for , so we do nothing).
  3. Increment (so that the CPU will be ready to fetch the next instruction on the next call to ).

So the upshot of all this is that if you call on a machine with pointing to a instruction, the state of the machine should be unchanged after it returns except that the register should hold a value one higher than before.

Uncomment and run the test, which does the following:

  1. Stores the instruction at address 0.
  2. Calls on the machine.
  3. Tests that the machine’s register contains the value 1. If not, the test fails with a message like

This test will not pass yet, because the method currently does nothing. Over to you to fix that!

Write the code in needed to make this test pass. You don’t need much!

You can solve this the “malicious compliance” way if you like, doing literally what the test asks for and no more. Right now the test is only concerned with the value of after calling .

We’ll extend the test later, of course, so if you want to get ahead a little, you could read the contents of memory at the address held by and use something like a statement (in Go) or a expression (in Rust) to decide what to do, as well as updating the value of .

If you’re stuck, or if you want to compare your answer with one suggested version, have a look at my Go solution, or the Rust solution.

You’ll find the TypeScript solutions to each challenge in Sebastián’s ts-r8-solutions repo.

It doesn’t matter if you’ve implemented in a slightly different way to these example solutions, as long as the test passes. After all, the real CPU on the spacecraft implements it using transistors! It’s the behaviour that matters with an emulator, not the implementation.

When the test is passing, you can go on to the next section. Or if you like, pause for tea and biscuits, and some deserved self-congratulation: you’ve written a working CPU emulator! Admittedly, so far it has a rather restricted instruction set, but that can soon be fixed.

Actually, if you were feeling lazy, you could have implemented by writing no more than this (in Go, for example):

You could do more, and if you have, that’s not wrong; but this is all the test actually requires. Since does nothing, and we know the instruction will be , we needn’t even read it from memory. And since the test only checks that is 1 afterwards, we can achieve that by just setting it to that value directly. It might look silly, but it takes the test seriously as the full specification of what it should do.

That’s fine, except we know the real method will need to do more than this. Let’s extend the test, then, so that we can no longer pass it the lazy way.

Extend to store instructions in the first two memory locations, and call , checking for the correct value of after each call. After the first , should be 1, as the test already checks. But after the second , it should be 2.

Adjust to make the test pass.

Updating the test is easy, but if you took the lazy route to implementing , now you’ll have to work a little harder. Even so, you don’t have to actually read the memory or look at the opcode—though you can if you want. The key thing as far as the test is concerned is that should increase by 1 every time is called.

Great. So your test is now executing the following (not particularly interesting, but valid) R8 program:

We could make this program longer, by adding more s, but we’d also need to have the test call again for each one. If we want to execute programs of length, we don’t really want to do it by repeatedly calling in the test.

We’d like a way to tell the CPU to just keep on fetching and executing continuously, as it does in reality. Of course the problem then is, what would make it ?

In reality, CPUs generally don’t stop; they always have work to do, even if it’s just updating the screen, taking care of background jobs like backups, and waiting for you to press a key or click the mouse. But for test purposes, it’ll be very handy for us to have an instruction that tells the CPU to stop work for now, and return control to the emulator. Let’s call it (opcode 0).

Now, what would do? Well, if you call , nothing special. After all, the machine already effectively halts after each call. But we’re saying we want a new method that, unlike , keeps fetching and executing continuously until it sees a instruction, at which point it returns. Let’s call this method (by which we really mean “run ”, of course).

What would a test for look like? You might like to think about this a bit and see if you can come up with something.

Try writing a test for ; don’t actually implement yet, just write an empty method. We want to make sure that the test fails when does nothing.

One way to do it would be to submit a program like this to the CPU:

If we called on this program, we should expect to increase by 2. If it increases by less, or not at all, then isn’t calling enough times. If it increases by too much, or never returns, then isn’t correctly detecting the instruction.

Okay, now let’s try to make the test pass!

We already have code that performs a single fetch-execute cycle, so we don’t need to duplicate it here. can simply call to do that work. The part that needs a little extra thought is this: how does know when to stop running? Or, equivalently, how can report the fact that it executed a instruction?

Again, you could solve this problem a completely different way than I have, and that’s fine. If the emulator correctly executes the test program, it’s correct.

Now we can both and the machine, it’s time to do a little refactoring. We’re going to be referring to opcodes a lot in the emulator, so it’ll be helpful to define some constants for them, with informative names. Here’s a homework problem for you while you’re eagerly awaiting the next instalment.

Define named constants for (0) and (1). Prefixing the names with helps remind readers what of value they are.

Refactor the tests and code to use these constants (for example, in the test, we should set the contents of address 0 to the named constant , instead of a literal .) This makes it easier for readers (including our future selves) to see what the test is doing.

Use the tests to make sure that your refactoring didn’t break anything. Check that you also used the constants in your method. If you like, change the values of the two constants to something different (99 and 100, say) and make sure that everything still passes (it should). Don’t forget to change them back afterwards.

If you get stuck, tune in next time to see the suggested solutions.

Great progress! Your emulator is now looking a lot more realistic: it can be single-stepped, or run until halted. All it needs now to be able to start writing useful programs is a few more opcodes, and we’ll get to those in the next part. If you want to skip ahead and learn a bit about the R8 architecture (and maybe implement more of its instructions), have a look at the RX82 project, which uses it to emulate a fantasy retro 8-bit computer from an alternate 1982.
